items.title: Sameer Jain appointed Chair, Aanchal Basur appointed Vice Chair of ICC India Arbitration Group
items.summary: ICC India , in consultation with the ICC International Court of Arbitration and its Secretariat, has appointed Sameer Jain , as Chair of the ICC India Arbitration Group, with Aanchal Basur appointed as Vice Chair, effective September 1, 2026. Jain is the Managing Partner at PSL Advocates & Solicitors and Basur is Partner at AB Law. Both Jain and Basur are members of the ICC Commission on Arbitration and ADR and formerly served as regional representatives of ICC’s Young Arbitration and ADR Forum from India. Jain previously served as a member of the IAG’s core committee, while Basur served as its Secretary. Sameer Jain succeeds Shashank Garg , under whose leadership the Group expanded its engagement with practitioners, in-house counsel, students and other stakeholders across the arbitration community. Speaking on the appointments, Claudia Salomon, President of the ICC International Court of Arbitration, said, “We are pleased to welcome Sameer and Aanchal to their new leadership roles within the ICC India Arbitration Group. items.title: Kerala High Court allows Christian women to file divorce pleas before courts in places where they reside
items.summary: The Kerala High Court on Wednesday held that Christian women can file for divorce before the family court having jurisdiction over the place where she resides, even if it is different from the place where her marriage was solemnised or where she last resided with her husband. A Division Bench of Justice AK Jayasankaran Nambiar and Justice Preeta AK held that a restrictive interpretation of Section 3(3) of the Divorce Act would be discriminative to christian women. Section 3(3) of the Divorce Act, which governs the dissolution of Christian marriages, sets out the territorial jurisdiction for filing a divorce petition. The Court said the provision should be interpreted in a manner which is consistent with the constitutional guarantees of gender equality. It added that similar provisions in the Hindu Marriage Act and the Special Marriage Act have already been amended to provide this relief for the married women covered by those laws. items.title: From Cambridge to Indian campuses, a similar playbook hounds the marginalised
items.summary: Early this year, we were in Manchester to attend the British Sociological Association’s 75th annual conference. Sitting among hundreds of academics, we were deeply intrigued by the title of Professor Jason Arday, the former Cambridge scholar’s plenary talk – ‘Wanted dead or alive: The playbook’. Arday, with great enthusiasm but also visible pain, laid it out for all of us. In a chillingly prophetic way, he discussed how Black, Asian, Minority and Ethnic community scholars who could establish themselves across elite educational institutions within the UK and the US have been on the academic ‘hitlist’ of far-right racist attacks, discrediting and hounding. In his speech, he remembered his Black colleagues who were subjected to institutional racism and media trials. Subsequently, some were forced to leave their prestigious jobs, while some took their own lives. His arguments warned us not to treat these experiences in isolation. Instead, through the ‘playbook’, he exposed the mechanisms of systemic hatred disguised as merit, scrutiny, procedures and academic standards. Recently, we woke up to the news of Arday’s death. items.title: The Meta episode: Why India’s IT platform rules need a right to restoration
items.summary: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology gave Mark Zuckerberg 3 days to tender an unqualified personal apology for the restriction of the Prime Minister's Facebook video between roughly 12:30 AM and 5 AM on July 28, 2026. Failing that, it recommended that the Union government consider withdrawing Meta's protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Most of the commentary since has asked whether the threat is executable. It is not; that can be disposed of briefly. The more useful question has gone largely unexamined. What does an intermediary owe a user whose lawful content it restricts and is that obligation enforceable by anyone at present? On the current text and practice, close to nothing. That is the defect this episode has exposed and no apology addresses it.
